titulo.texto: The Museum and Tlaltecuhtli in the Lobby

frase_gancho.texto: A twelve-ton earth goddess welcomes everyone who enters the museum.

puente_narrativo.texto: When you’re ready, continue to the next stop on your tour.

guion_largo.texto:
Welcome to the Templo Mayor Museum. Before entering the halls, there are two things worth knowing: how this building came to be, and which piece greets you in the lobby.

The museum opened on October twelfth, nineteen eighty-seven. The project was by the architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, with Javier Ramírez Campuzano. It was built next to the ruins, as a result of the Templo Mayor Project, to display the objects recovered in the excavations. It has eight halls. The first ones provide context, then come those devoted to the two shrines, to tribute, and to nature, and the last one deals with the conquest and what came after. It is best to follow that order, because it tells a story.

In the lobby, Tlaltecuhtli awaits you. Its name is usually translated as lord or lady of the earth. In the Mexica tradition, the earth was seen as a living force, one that gave life and also received the dead. That is why its image is one of the most powerful in the pantheon.

The sculpture appeared on October second, two thousand six. It measures four meters seventeen by three meters sixty-two, and weighs close to twelve tons, according to INAH. It was an enormous and fragile piece, and its restoration took three years. Because of its size, moving and studying it was a considerable technical challenge. It preserves traces of its original polychromy, that is, the color with which it was painted in its day.

It is dated between fifteen oh two and fifteen twenty-one, that is, to the final years of the empire. According to the archaeologist Eduardo Matos Moctezuma, the worship of Tlaltecuhtli was restricted to priests. That is, it was not an image for the general public, and that makes it even more interesting.

Today you see it in full light and up close, in the lobby of a museum. That is a way of seeing it that its creators surely never had in mind. Take a moment to look at it calmly, from different angles, before entering the halls. There is no rush: it is one of the largest pieces in the museum and one of those that deserve the most time.

As you observe it, notice the details of the surface: the reliefs, the forms that repeat, and the traces of color. If the museum offers an explanation on a wall label, read it, because it helps you recognize the elements of the figure.

One last point. This piece shows how archaeology keeps discovering things, even in a city as thoroughly explored as this one. Barely two decades ago, no one knew that Tlaltecuhtli lay underground. With that idea in mind, move on to the halls. There you will find objects that have been hidden for centuries, and that came out of the earth thanks to the excavations you already know about.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Tlaltecuhtli was a public image, seen by everyone.
